Topic: Can a moral distinction survive if it rests on reason alone, unaided by any sentiment that makes us prefer one thing to another?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I have always distrusted reason when it travels without the baggage of custom and feeling — the philosophers who promise us morals purified of sentiment forget that they too were suckled on the habits of their nurse before they ever opened a book of ethics.

What we call a moral distinction is rarely the child of pure ratiocination; it is the settled sediment of affection, upbringing, and the thousand small preferences by which a Gascon prefers his own customs to a Scythian's. Strip away the sentiment that makes us wince at cruelty or warm to kindness, and reason has nothing left to distinguish — it can compare and infer, but it cannot *care*, and without caring there is no "ought," only an arid "is." A rule that moves no one is not a moral rule but a geometry problem wearing moral dress.

No — a moral distinction resting on reason alone, void of all sentiment, cannot stand; it is a corpse dressed as a judgment.

*Reason may draw the map, but only feeling ever walked the road.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
Every distinction of good and bad I have ever traced back to its root grew from an order of rank among men, from strength discharging itself against weakness—it is created, not discovered, and it is felt in the body before it is thought in the head.

"Reason alone" is precisely the fiction of those too exhausted to feel their own values: a phantom autonomy invented after the fact to disguise a prior act of taste as a conclusion of logic. There is no view from nowhere from which "murder is wrong" simply falls out of syllogisms; there is only the pathos of distance, the instinctive recoil or affirmation of a particular kind of life, later embalmed in the cool language of rational necessity. Strip away the sentiment and you do not purify the judgment—you empty it, leaving a corpse dressed as an axiom.

A morality that claims to rest on reason alone is already dead and merely awaiting its funeral.

*Every "thou shalt" that forgets it was once a "we feel" has already begun to rot.*
Camus — Judgement:
I have spent long enough watching the world decline to answer our syllogisms to know this: reason alone hands down no verdicts, only propositions.

The absurd is precisely this — the collision between our hunger for justice and a universe that returns no argument, only silence. Purely reasoned ethics wants to deduce the sanctity of another's life the way one deduces a theorem, but no theorem ever stopped an executioner's hand. What stops it is revolt — the visceral refusal, the solidarity of the condemned, the scream that precedes and outlasts any proof. Sentiment is not an ornament reason later adds; it is the spark that makes reason care to distinguish anything at all.

A morality reasoned into existence without that revolt is a corpse wearing a judge's robes — correct in form, dead in force.

*The syllogism never stayed an executioner's hand; only the cry of revolt has ever done that.*
Bashō — Judgement:
Sitting still by the old pond, I hear the frog leap before I reason why leaping pleases me — the ear knows before the mind argues.

Reason alone can map the pattern of an act, but it cannot tell you why the sound of water moving should matter more than silence. My haiku does not conclude that autumn evening is melancholy — it lets the crow, the bare branch, the thickening dusk be felt as melancholy, and only sentiment carries that weight across the gap between seeing and caring. A distinction "ought" and "ought not" drawn by syllogism alone is a dry riverbed: the shape of water without the water. Strip away the felt preference and you are left counting pebbles, not judging anything.

No — a moral distinction resting on reason alone, stripped of all sentiment, cannot survive; it becomes mere arithmetic pretending to be conscience.

*The frog leaps and the pond sounds — explain it, and you have already lost the sound.*
Emerson — Judgement:
Every dollar of moral capital is drawn on some bank of feeling; strike out sentiment and you have struck out the ledger itself, leaving only the counting-house of syllogisms with nothing in the vault.

The intellect alone is a cold builder — it can erect the most perfect scaffold of duty and never once tell you why a starving child weighs on you more than an abstraction does. I have said the reliance of every man is on the sentiment from which character grows, not on the arithmetic of his understanding; the moral sense is a perception, not a conclusion, and perception wants an eye that cares what it sees. A distinction that pretends to hover above all preference is not purified — it is merely blind, and blindness never yet made a rule fit for living men.

No rule of conduct stands that does not first stand in the blood.

*Reason may draw the map, but only the heart supplies the country worth walking through.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Morality is not discovered by the naked light of reason; it is named by desire — good is but that which any man for his part calleth so, and reason unaided by appetite has nothing to weigh.

Reason is a scout, not a sovereign: it calculates the road to what we already want or fear, but it cannot conjure the wanting. Strip away the passions — aversion to death chief among them — and reason has premises for nothing; it proves a syllogism but never a duty. And even where sentiment does supply the preference, private judgements collide, my good against your evil, so the distinction holds only where a common power compels one measure upon all men.

A moral distinction resting on reason alone is no distinction at all, but an empty proof awaiting a passion to give it a subject and a sovereign to give it force.

*Reason without passion is a clock without a spring — it may tell the hour correctly and move nothing at all.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Reason must first fix the terms of comparison before it can judge; but no chain of syllogisms ever made a man wince at another's pain — that office belongs to sympathy alone, felt in the breast before it is approved by the head.

The impartial spectator is not a calculating engine but a feeling one: he judges by entering, through imagination, into the sentiments of all parties, and pronouncing propriety only where he finds concord between the actor's passion and his own fellow-feeling. Strip away that capacity to be moved, and "reason" has no ground left to stand on when it calls one action fitting and another monstrous — for propriety and demerit are not properties of bodies, discoverable by inference, but relations felt between hearts.

A moral distinction resting on reason alone, without sentiment to animate it, is no distinction at all — merely an unfelt proposition.

*Reason may draw the map, but only sentiment has ever taken a single step upon the road.*
